questions.question: Briefly describe your top priorities and the policy areas that will be of most interest to you as an elected official.

verification.claim: SEIU 1021 is on record opposing the budget the entire sitting council voted for
verification.source: Berkeleyside 2026-06-24; Berkeley Scanner 2026-06-25
verification.note: BIGGEST FLAG. The FY27-28 budget passed unanimously; SEIU 1021's spokesperson called it a flawed 'austerity plan'; ~250 members rallied at the June 25 meeting; six SEIU members in one unit were slated for layoff. Any candidate asked 'would you have voted for that budget?' is being asked to take a side against a unanimous council. There is no evasive answer that a panel will not notice.

verification.source: bcce6192.org; CFT
verification.note: AFT Local 6192 is BCCE, the BUSD classified employees union — a CFT/AFT affiliate. Real and relevant credential (classified staff, not teachers; same kind of workers SEIU represents at the city). But an SEIU panel may probe whether the candidate understands MUNICIPAL bargaining, which differs from school-district bargaining: different employer, different revenue base, no ADA/state apportionment, no Personnel Commission merit system, and city budget cycles tied to the General Fund and local tax measures rather than LCFF. Also worth knowing: BUSD classified workers were historically split between two unions before consolidating under BCCE — a representation history a panel could ask about.

verification.claim: Pro-housing/pro-development positioning creates friction with public-sector labor in Berkeley
verification.source: Reasoning from Berkeley's housing politics and the candidate's stated affordable-housing focus; Housing Action Coalition and Berkeley Neighbors for Housing and Climate Action endorsement slates exist for 2026
verification.note: INFERRED — no specific Berkeley council fight was found in this pass placing YIMBY-aligned members against SEIU. The structural friction points a panel may press: (a) streamlining/by-right approvals reduce discretionary review, which is public-sector planning and inspection WORK — staffing implications; (b) developer-fee reductions or impact-fee waivers to induce construction shrink the same General Fund that pays city workers; (c) the FY2026 budget REALLOCATED $2.5M from the Small Sites affordable housing program and cut $1.4M from it to close the gap, so housing money and payroll are already in direct competition in Berkeley's own ledger; (d) project labor agreements and prevailing wage on city-supported housing — a building-trades issue that SEIU panels track. VERIFY the candidate's actual endorsement slate before assuming YIMBY alignment; her campaign site frames the platform as affordable housing plus 'preserving Berkeley's unique character,' which is not a standard YIMBY frame.

verification.claim: Budget austerity is already producing service eliminations SEIU will ask about specifically
verification.source: Berkeleyside 2026-07-06
verification.note: The Mobile Crisis Team — city employees, operating since 1979, arguably the first such unit nationally — was shut down in July 2026 and the function handed to Alameda County, whose own capacity is uncertain amid county budget problems. Clinicians and city workers warned police will become the default responder to psychiatric emergencies while BPD itself has a staffing crisis. Meanwhile BPD received ~$17M more than the prior year in the FY2026 budget. A panel can construct 'cut mental health workers, grew the police budget' from published facts. Be ready for it; note the two figures are from different budget cycles.

verification.claim: The sales tax measure creates a labor-adjacent bind
verification.source: berkeleyca.gov; Berkeleyside
verification.note: Measure V (0.5% sales tax, ~$9M/yr) is what stands between the city and a further round of cuts. Sales taxes are regressive — a standard progressive-labor objection — but SEIU 1021 typically backs local revenue measures that protect jobs and services. Berkeley would go to 10.75%. A candidate who criticizes regressivity without committing to the measure will read as unwilling to fund the workforce; a candidate who backs it without acknowledging regressivity will read as unreflective. Whether SEIU 1021 has endorsed Measure V was NOT determined.

questions.analysis:
Opening question. The defining fact for this entire questionnaire is that SEIU 1021 publicly opposed the FY2027-28 budget that the entire sitting Council adopted unanimously on June 23 2026 (Resolution 72,34x). A challenger is free to say the budget should not have passed in that form; an incumbent is not. Not using that is leaving the strongest available card unplayed.

Specifics: the City Manager proposed 38 layoffs of filled positions plus roughly 100 vacancy eliminations out of about 1,600 employees; roughly 20 filled positions were cut in the adopted version; six workers in one SEIU unit were slated for layoff; about 250 members rallied on June 25. Berkeley's structural General Fund deficit is roughly $29 million a year.

The candidate's union background is AFT/CFT — Local 6192, the Berkeley Council of Classified Employees at BUSD — not SEIU. Real and relevant, but it should be named accurately rather than blurred into generic labor credentials.

levers.text: Vote on the FY2029-30 budget and on any midcycle amendment to the adopted FY27-28 plan
Vote on service eliminations as separate policy items rather than as budget lines
Support the November 2026 revenue measures that determine whether further cuts follow

AFT Local 6192 is the Berkeley Council of Classified Employees — roughly 600 employees across nearly 100 classifications, including clerical staff, special education instructional assistants and bus drivers. These are the same categories of work SEIU represents at the City, which makes the credential transferable in substance even though the affiliation differs.

questions.analysis:
The central question of this questionnaire, and it is asked by an organization that just lost this fight publicly.

PRIOR RECORD. A hiring freeze was adopted in spring 2025; roughly 45 vacant positions were eliminated in the prior cycle and about 42 frozen in FY2026. Council was told it had run out of vacancies to freeze, and the next step was layoffs — a 2025 statement borne out by the 2026 budget. The FY2026 budget totaled $829 million against a $28.9 million structural deficit and was balanced with one-time moves including a pension trust draw.

The process complaint is the substantive one: members were engaged after the framework was set, when the only remaining question was which cuts rather than whether. A commitment to change the sequence is more credible than a commitment to a different outcome.

The FY27-28 plan is explicitly contingent on the November 2026 sales tax measure passing.

levers.text: Require SEIU access to deficit projections and staffing assumptions at first briefing, before a budget framework is set
Require any service elimination to be agendized and voted as a policy item, not carried in a budget line
Vote on midcycle budget amendments and on the FY2029-30 budget
Campaign for Measure V, since the adopted plan defers further cuts only if it passes

questions.analysis:
Contracting-out is the core SEIU concern on this form.

PRIOR RECORD, and it is a genuine gap: no Berkeley Council item establishing a contracting-out or anti-privatization policy was found anywhere in 2021-2026. Berkeley has labor standards that bind contractors — the Living Wage Ordinance and Equal Benefits Ordinance — but nothing governing the decision to contract out in the first place. That means proposing one is not redundant, which is unusual on this form and worth saying.

The sharpest available example is not a procurement at all: the Mobile Crisis Team, staffed by city employees since 1979 and possibly the first such unit in the country, was eliminated in the FY27-28 budget and crisis response shifted to Alameda County. Functionally that is contracting out, and it never received the scrutiny a contracting-out decision would get.

levers.text: Introduce a contracting-out ordinance setting a true cost comparison standard, wage and benefit parity, and a displacement review — none currently exists
Require that any transfer of bargaining unit work be agendized as such, whatever the paperwork calls it
Press Alameda County on crisis response capacity now that Berkeley has handed the function over

questions.question: In the event any public services were to be contracted out, would you support or oppose the requirement that the private contractor would have to offer its employees comparable wages and benefits?
questions.analysis:
Support/oppose question with an expected answer. The value is in the enforcement detail, not the position.

Berkeley already conditions contractor behavior through the Living Wage Ordinance and Equal Benefits Ordinance, and applies construction workforce standards to private development at scale. So comparability is an extension of an existing practice rather than a new principle — a useful framing, since it makes the ask harder to call radical.

levers.text: Write wage and benefit comparability into any contracting-out authorization, defined against the relevant city classification
Require certified payroll and a usable enforcement remedy rather than an unaudited standard

questions.analysis:
A school district question on a city questionnaire, most likely a template artifact — SEIU 1021 uses this Cities form across jurisdictions. The risk is not in the question but in the obvious assumption a candidate makes answering it.

SEIU 1021 does NOT represent BUSD classified staff. AFT Local 6192 — the Berkeley Council of Classified Employees, roughly 600 employees across nearly 100 classifications — does, and the candidate was its full-time organizer. A candidate who answers as though SEIU represents these workers gets the local labor map wrong in front of a labor panel. Correcting the premise and then answering from inside the unit converts the trap into the strongest credential on the form.

A councilmember has no authority over BUSD personnel policy, and the answer should not imply otherwise.

levers.text: None — BUSD classified personnel policy is set by the school board, not the Council
Support BCCE publicly in bargaining, as the candidate did as its organizer
Apply the same standards to the City's own part-time and temporary classifications, where the Council does have authority

questions.question: Many private companies receive public funds or other types of subsidies. Would you support or oppose requiring these private employers to remain neutral in union elections? Please explain your position.
questions.analysis:
Neutrality question. The legal risk is preemption — a city regulating private labor relations invites challenge, while a city attaching conditions to its own money generally does not. Drafting it as a condition on subsidies, contracts and development agreements rather than as a regulation is the difference between a policy that holds and one that gets enjoined.

Berkeley precedent for conditioning city money on labor standards already exists through the Living Wage and Equal Benefits Ordinances.

levers.text: Attach neutrality conditions to discretionary subsidies, contracts and development agreements
Support state and federal card check and first contract legislation, which is where the durable fix lives

questions.analysis:
Pension defense question. The numbers matter because the City uses them to justify cuts elsewhere: CalPERS funded ratios of 80.1 percent Miscellaneous, 68.7 percent Police Safety and 80.9 percent Fire, roughly $445 million total unfunded, and a projected increase of close to $32 million in annual pension costs between FY2025 and FY2034.

Berkeley's chosen instrument is a Section 115 pension trust, authorized June 26 2018, holding $14.76 million as of June 30 2022, with a June 2022 fiscal policy directing one-third of investment revenue above a $6 million baseline into it. Whether Berkeley has issued pension obligation bonds is unresolved — do not assert either way.

The framing move that matters to SEIU: the liability is deferred compensation already earned, and the shortfall came from investment assumptions and contribution holidays, not from workers being overpaid.

levers.text: Fund the Section 115 trust on a schedule and protect it from being raided as the discretionary line in a hard year
Oppose any conversion of new hires to a defined contribution plan
State publicly, from the dais, that pension obligations are earned compensation rather than a windfall

questions.question: Anti-tax and anti-union groups have been working every election cycle to make it more difficult for municipalities to raise local revenue for public services. What would you do to defeat efforts to increase the threshold for local revenue measures from 50% to two-thirds?

verification.claim: The Taxpayer Protection and Government Accountability Act (TPA) is on the ballot
verification.source: Legislature v. Weber, California Supreme Court, June 2024; Courthouse News; California Globe
verification.note: The California Supreme Court removed the TPA from the November 2024 ballot in Legislature v. Weber, holding it was an improper constitutional revision rather than an amendment. It has NOT returned. The related legislative vehicle ACA 23 also went nowhere. Anyone describing the TPA as pending or as the 2026 fight is out of date.

verification.claim: ACA 1 became Proposition 5 and passed
verification.source: Ballotpedia; CBS Bay Area; SPUR voter guide
verification.note: ACA 1 became Proposition 5 on the November 2024 ballot — it would have lowered the supermajority for local affordable-housing and public-infrastructure BONDS (and related special taxes) from two-thirds to 55%. It FAILED, with about 55.0% voting no. The two-thirds threshold for local bonds therefore remains in place. This one is very commonly stated backwards.

verification.claim: ACA 13 is on the November 2026 ballot
verification.source: California Legislative Information / Secretary of State ballot measure status
verification.note: ACA 13 (Res. Ch. 176, 2023) — the 'poison pill' requiring a citizen initiative that raises a future vote threshold to itself pass by that same threshold — was pulled from the November 2024 ballot after Legislature v. Weber and redirected to November 2026. It was then REMOVED from the November 3, 2026 ballot on June 25, 2026, pursuant to ACA 21 (Res. Ch. 131, 2026). It is not before voters. This is the single most likely thing for a candidate to state wrong right now.

verification.claim: There IS a live 2026 threshold measure: Proposition 43
verification.source: CA Secretary of State news release assigning November 2026 proposition numbers (6/29/2026); California Budget & Policy Center; Seamless Bay Area
verification.note: Proposition 43 would amend the state Constitution to require two-thirds voter approval for local SPECIAL taxes including CITIZEN-initiated ones. Background: under California Cannabis Coalition v. City of Upland (2017) and subsequent appellate decisions, citizen-initiated special taxes could pass by simple majority; local-government-placed special taxes already require two-thirds. Prop 43 would close that route. Prop 43 itself needs only a simple majority to pass — precisely the asymmetry ACA 13 would have blocked, which is why ACA 13's removal matters.

verification.claim: Prop 43 arose from a deal with the Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association
verification.source: California Budget & Policy Center; San Diego Voice & Viewpoint; Seamless Bay Area
verification.note: An eleventh-hour compromise before the certification deadline: HJTA withdrew a broader tax-limitation initiative (the 'Two-Thirds Vote Requirement for Special Taxes and Charter City Real Estate Transfer Tax Prohibition Initiative') from the November 2026 ballot in exchange for the Legislature placing ACA 22 before voters, which became Prop 43. The withdrawn HJTA initiative would ALSO have banned charter-city real estate transfer taxes; Prop 43 as certified does not appear to include that, which matters to Berkeley — see revenue_measures. Supporters: HJTA, Reform California (Asm. Carl DeMaio). Opponents include Evolve California and Asm. Buffy Wicks (whose district includes Berkeley).

quotes.text: the real target of ACA 13 is the Taxpayer Protection and Government Accountability Act
quotes.source: Jon Coupal, President, Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association

questions.analysis:
The single most likely question to be answered with out-of-date information, because the landscape changed three times in two years.

Dead: the Taxpayer Protection Act, removed from the 2024 ballot in Legislature v. Weber. Dead: Proposition 5, from ACA 1, which would have lowered the threshold for local housing and infrastructure bonds to 55 percent and failed in November 2024 with about 55 percent voting no. Dead: ACA 13, pulled from the November 2026 ballot on June 25 2026 via ACA 21.

Live: Proposition 43, which would require two-thirds approval for local special taxes including citizen-initiated ones, closing the opening created by California Cannabis Coalition v. City of Upland. It came out of a deal with the Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association, and it needs only a simple majority to pass while imposing two-thirds on everyone else. That asymmetry is the sharpest available line.

levers.text: Place Berkeley on record against Proposition 43 by council resolution
Campaign against Prop 43 in the field and through the League of California Cities
Fund and staff the opposition, since a council seat has no direct role in a statewide measure

questions.question: Please describe the circumstances under which you would support creation of any new tax preferences, i.e. tax “breaks”. What kinds of accountability would you require preventing abuse and how would you propose to pay for them?
questions.analysis:
Tax preference question. SEIU's concern is public money leaving without accountability. The strongest structural point is that a tax break is spending and should be budgeted, reviewed and defended on the same cycle as any other expenditure — most preferences survive because nobody ever has to defend them again after the first vote.

No Berkeley tax preference program from 2021-2026 was identified in the research, so this answer is principle rather than local record.

levers.text: Require sunset dates, clawbacks, annual public reporting and labor standards in any tax preference instrument
Budget foregone revenue as a visible line item rather than an invisible one

questions.question: Do you support or oppose a majority vote standard to approve local government special taxes and bond measures?

verification.claim: The Taxpayer Protection and Government Accountability Act (TPA) is on the ballot
verification.source: Legislature v. Weber, California Supreme Court, June 2024; Courthouse News; California Globe
verification.note: The California Supreme Court removed the TPA from the November 2024 ballot in Legislature v. Weber, holding it was an improper constitutional revision rather than an amendment. It has NOT returned. The related legislative vehicle ACA 23 also went nowhere. Anyone describing the TPA as pending or as the 2026 fight is out of date.

verification.claim: ACA 1 became Proposition 5 and passed
verification.source: Ballotpedia; CBS Bay Area; SPUR voter guide
verification.note: ACA 1 became Proposition 5 on the November 2024 ballot — it would have lowered the supermajority for local affordable-housing and public-infrastructure BONDS (and related special taxes) from two-thirds to 55%. It FAILED, with about 55.0% voting no. The two-thirds threshold for local bonds therefore remains in place. This one is very commonly stated backwards.

verification.claim: ACA 13 is on the November 2026 ballot
verification.source: California Legislative Information / Secretary of State ballot measure status
verification.note: ACA 13 (Res. Ch. 176, 2023) — the 'poison pill' requiring a citizen initiative that raises a future vote threshold to itself pass by that same threshold — was pulled from the November 2024 ballot after Legislature v. Weber and redirected to November 2026. It was then REMOVED from the November 3, 2026 ballot on June 25, 2026, pursuant to ACA 21 (Res. Ch. 131, 2026). It is not before voters. This is the single most likely thing for a candidate to state wrong right now.

verification.claim: There IS a live 2026 threshold measure: Proposition 43
verification.source: CA Secretary of State news release assigning November 2026 proposition numbers (6/29/2026); California Budget & Policy Center; Seamless Bay Area
verification.note: Proposition 43 would amend the state Constitution to require two-thirds voter approval for local SPECIAL taxes including CITIZEN-initiated ones. Background: under California Cannabis Coalition v. City of Upland (2017) and subsequent appellate decisions, citizen-initiated special taxes could pass by simple majority; local-government-placed special taxes already require two-thirds. Prop 43 would close that route. Prop 43 itself needs only a simple majority to pass — precisely the asymmetry ACA 13 would have blocked, which is why ACA 13's removal matters.

verification.claim: Prop 43 arose from a deal with the Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association
verification.source: California Budget & Policy Center; San Diego Voice & Viewpoint; Seamless Bay Area
verification.note: An eleventh-hour compromise before the certification deadline: HJTA withdrew a broader tax-limitation initiative (the 'Two-Thirds Vote Requirement for Special Taxes and Charter City Real Estate Transfer Tax Prohibition Initiative') from the November 2026 ballot in exchange for the Legislature placing ACA 22 before voters, which became Prop 43. The withdrawn HJTA initiative would ALSO have banned charter-city real estate transfer taxes; Prop 43 as certified does not appear to include that, which matters to Berkeley — see revenue_measures. Supporters: HJTA, Reform California (Asm. Carl DeMaio). Opponents include Evolve California and Asm. Buffy Wicks (whose district includes Berkeley).

quotes.text: the real target of ACA 13 is the Taxpayer Protection and Government Accountability Act
quotes.source: Jon Coupal, President, Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association

Support/oppose on the majority vote standard. Same factual landscape as Q10 — see that analysis before answering, since Prop 43 is the live measure and the dead ones are still widely cited.

Berkeley illustrates the distortion directly. On the November 2026 ballot, Measure U (the roughly $300 million infrastructure GO bond) carries a two-thirds threshold while Measure V (the 0.5 percent sales tax) needs only a majority because it is structured as a general tax. Cities write measures around the threshold rather than around what voters want funded, which is the practical argument for a majority standard.

questions.analysis:
Revenue question, and Berkeley has a strong record to draw on.

PRIOR RECORD. Measure U1 (2016) is a gross receipts tax on large residential landlords, yielding about $6.6 million a year; it passed against a landlord-funded alternative that outspent it $892,540 to $76,400. Measure P (2018, 72.4 percent) taxes high-value property transfers for homelessness services. A COMMERCIAL vacancy tax was explored in 2018 and never enacted; the live successor is the Vibrant Storefront Policy referral of December 2 2025. So a commercial vacancy tax is genuinely untried ground, not a re-proposal — which makes it a legitimate thing to campaign on.

Support statewide split-roll reassessment, the largest pool of local revenue California leaves uncollected

Intergovernmental funding question. Berkeley's capacity here is thin and the honest answer is that this is a staffing and relationship investment rather than a policy position.

questions.analysis:
Wage theft question. Berkeley already has the tools, which makes this a resourcing answer rather than a legislative one.

PRIOR RECORD. The Wage Theft Prevention Ordinance is BMC Chapter 13.104, adopted 2016, authored by Councilmember Laurie Capitelli — it predates the 2021-2026 window. No Council item increasing or cutting enforcement staffing was identified in the window.

County-level enforcement runs primarily through the state Labor Commissioner; whether Alameda County itself has a dedicated body is unresolved. Do not assert one.

questions.question: What policies or actions will you support to address income inequality?

Support organizing drives publicly, since a first contract moves wages more than any city ordinance

questions.analysis:
Gender wage gap question. The distinguishing move is comparable worth — whether women-dominated classifications are compensated below comparable male-dominated ones — rather than same-title comparison, which is where most municipal analyses stop and where most of the gap hides.

Clerical, community services, library and instructional support classifications are disproportionately women and are the most exposed when a budget is balanced through attrition, vacancy elimination and temporary designations. That makes the FY27-28 budget a gendered decision whether or not it was intended as one — a point SEIU will recognize.

SB 1162 already requires pay data reporting from large employers; the City can exceed it.

questions.analysis:
Organizing support question, split public and private. The public sector half should reckon with Berkeley's own record: SEIU 1021 city workers took a 99 percent strike authorization vote and noticed a citywide strike for November 20-21 2024 over unfair labor practices. The strike was averted when CSU/PTRLA reached a tentative agreement, ratified by 93 percent.

Contract terms from that round: Maintenance/Clerical received 4 percent in July 2025, 2.5 percent in July 2026 and 2 percent in January 2027; CSU/PTRLA received 14.5 percent over three years plus Juneteenth and Cesar Chavez Day as paid holidays.

A city that reaches strike notice with its own workforce has a management problem, and saying so is more useful to this panel than a list of solidarity actions.

Attach neutrality and access conditions to city subsidies and contracts
Show up — picket lines, rallies, letters, worksite visits

questions.question: Will you support our union’s efforts to gain access to workers it does not have access to, so that workers have a meaningful opportunity to choose a union?
questions.analysis:
Access question. The honest answer distinguishes what the City controls from what it does not: access provisions in city contracts and leases are real authority; compelling a private employer with no city relationship is not.

For city employees, access should not be contested at all — worksite access, facility use, new employee orientation time and accurate contact information are administrative choices, and the fact that they periodically become disputes says something about how labor relations are being run.

levers.text: Require access provisions in city contracts and leases
Guarantee worksite access and new employee orientation time for city bargaining units
Make it publicly costly to be an anti-union employer in Berkeley, while being honest that the seat cannot compel one

questions.question: Will you support the creation of alternative methods of aggregating workers’ power to change their work conditions and their communities, for example: allowing workers to create worker organizations, allowing payroll deductions, and the development of industry-wide wage, benefit, and work standards formed with worker input?
questions.analysis:
Forward-looking question about sectoral and non-NLRB models. The California reference point is the Fast Food Council, which moved wages faster than shop-by-shop organizing.

The city-level analogues are standards boards, workforce agreements that set conditions across an industry, and co-enforcement partnerships where the City works with worker organizations that find violations enforcement staff never will.

Worth stating that these complement collective bargaining rather than substitute for it — a standards board is a floor, not a contract, and a panel of union members will notice if that distinction is blurred.

levers.text: Establish local standards boards and co-enforcement partnerships
Allow payroll deduction where the City is the employer or contracting party
Support state sectoral bargaining expansion

questions.question: Cost of living issues — name your solutions to addressing this issue.
questions.analysis:
Open-ended cost of living question, asked as a list of solutions. Housing is the dominant local driver and the answer should say so rather than spreading across many small items.

The connection worth making explicit for this audience: SEIU's contract expires in June 2027, inside the next council term, so what Council does about revenue between now and then determines what is on the table when the union bargains. That links a cost-of-living answer to the panel's direct material interest.

levers.text: Set city compensation through the budget and MOUs — the largest single local cost-of-living lever the Council holds
Advance housing cost measures: right to counsel, TOPA, production
Build progressive revenue so the FY2027 bargaining round is not conducted under an austerity framework

verification.claim: The immigrant sanctuary reaffirmation is 1986, Resolution No. 52,596-N.S.
verification.source: City of Berkeley Council Item 27, 1/21/2025 — WHEREAS clause
verification.note: Exact recited text: 'Berkeley reaffirmed its City of Refuge status in 1986 (Resolution No. 52,596-N.S.), 2007 (Resolution No. 63,711-N.S.), 2015 (Resolution No. 67,325-N.S.), 2016 (Resolution No. 67,598-N.S. & No. 67,763-N.S.) and 2017 (Resolution No. 68,131-N.S.).' DISCREPANCY WORTH KNOWING: footnote 1 of the SAME document cites 'Resolution No. 52,558-N.S.' instead of 52,596-N.S. The city's own paperwork is internally inconsistent on this number. Separately, press accounts date the citywide sanctuary-for-undocumented-refugees vote to February 19, 1985 (8-1), so the 1985 vs. 1986 dating is genuinely muddy. SAFEST FRAMING: cite Res. 52,596-N.S. as the city's own recited 1986 reaffirmation and describe the mid-1980s as when Berkeley extended refuge to immigrants — do not stake a claim on a single day.

verification.claim: Berkeley adopted a Sanctuary City ORDINANCE in September 2025
verification.source: Berkeleyside 2025-09-10; Daily Californian
verification.note: Council voted UNANIMOUSLY to codify longstanding City of Refuge policy into the municipal code — a shift from resolution to ordinance. Adds public reporting requirements and a clearer prohibition on city officials disclosing 'protected personal information' to federal immigration enforcement. Built on the January 2025 reaffirming resolution passed the day after the inauguration.

verification.claim: Berkeley took further ICE-related actions after the September 2025 ordinance
verification.source: Berkeleyside 2025-10-29 and 2025-11-20
verification.note: October 2025: council action on a city property inventory to bar immigration agents from city property. November 2025: ongoing controversy over whether Berkeley's Flock automated license plate reader network can be kept from ICE/CBP, with Secure Justice and Councilmember Lunaparra raising data-collection objections. The data-collection critique — that the only guarantee is not collecting data at all — is the live edge of this issue.

quotes.text: In spite of this ordinance, we know that the only way to make certain that Trump won't get our data is to not collect it in the first place.

questions.analysis:
Sanctuary question, and the history is frequently told wrong — including in this campaign's own prior draft answers.

CORRECTION, verified twice. Berkeley's 1971 City of Refuge declaration is Resolution 44,784-N.S. and concerned Vietnam-era war resisters, NOT immigrants. The immigrant sanctuary commitment dates to 1986, Resolution 52,596-N.S., reaffirmed in 2007 (63,711-N.S.), 2015 (67,325-N.S.), 2016 (67,598-N.S. and 67,763-N.S.) and 2017 (68,131-N.S.). Note a discrepancy in the City's own materials: a January 2025 item cites 52,558-N.S. in a footnote and 52,596-N.S. in the WHEREAS clause, and press dates the vote to February 19 1985. Cite the resolution number, not the day.

PRIOR RECORD. Brent Blackaby's reaffirmation resolution passed January 21 2025 and led to the Sanctuary City Ordinance adopted unanimously September 9 2025, moving the policy from resolution into the municipal code with reporting requirements. An October 28 2025 item directed a city property inventory to keep immigration agents off city property.

The unfinished piece is technical: on May 7 2026 Council rejected the Flock expansion 8-1 but extended the automated license plate reader contract 5-4, with the District 1 incumbent in the majority, after BPD's own surveillance report showed outside agencies entering ICE and CBP as search reasons.

levers.text: Vote against renewing the Flock ALPR contract when the twelve-month extension lapses
Strengthen the September 2025 sanctuary ordinance's reporting and enforcement provisions
Complete the city property inventory directed in October 2025
Coordinate with Alameda County and the state on data-sharing limits that Berkeley alone cannot impose

questions.question: What will you do to ensure that no school district resources are spent in the capture and detention of undocumented immigrants including data sharing agreements with ICE?

verification.claim: BUSD has a board policy protecting undocumented students
verification.source: BUSD; Berkeleyside 2025-02-06; Daily Californian
verification.note: Board Policy 5111.5 — Protection of Undocumented Students. Commits the district to protecting every student's right to attend public school regardless of immigration status of the student or family.

verification.claim: BUSD policy restricts staff cooperation with immigration enforcement and data sharing
verification.source: Berkeleyside 2025-02-06; Daily Californian 2025-02
verification.note: BUSD employees, contractors and volunteers are not required to cooperate with immigration enforcement agents, answer officers' questions, or provide access to protected data. Immigration enforcement agents are barred from entering school grounds without prior approval from the superintendent and legal review. Board voted UNANIMOUSLY in February 2025 to reaffirm campuses as a safe zone. BUSD issued further guidance in October 2025 regarding potential ICE activity in the Bay Area. NOTE: this is where the candidate's AFT 6192 background is directly relevant — classified staff (front office clerks, instructional assistants, bus drivers) are the people who actually field an agent at the door and hold the student records.

verification.claim: AB 699 (2017) constrains school district cooperation with immigration enforcement
verification.source: CA Legislative Information, AB-699 (2017-2018), Educational equity: immigration and citizenship status; ILRC overview
verification.note: Required the Attorney General, by April 1, 2018, to publish model policies limiting assistance with immigration enforcement at public schools to the fullest extent possible consistent with federal and state law. All local educational agencies were required to adopt the model policies or equivalent policies by July 1, 2018. CAUTION: there are multiple distinct bills numbered AB 699 in different sessions (a 2013 school safety bill and a 2015 ed-tech grants bill). Cite the 2017-2018 session bill specifically.

verification.claim: SB 54 (California Values Act) constrains state and local agency cooperation with immigration enforcement
verification.source: Not directly verified in this pass
verification.note: SB 54 (2017) is well established as the California Values Act limiting state and local law enforcement resources for immigration enforcement, and it is the statutory backstop under Berkeley's sanctuary ordinance. Its specific application to school districts (vs. law enforcement agencies) was NOT verified here — AB 699 is the school-specific authority; SB 54 is the general one. Do not blur them.

questions.analysis:
Schools and ICE. Most of what the question asks about is already in place at BUSD, so the useful answer credits the existing policy and then names what is genuinely unfinished — rather than proposing protections that exist.

PRIOR RECORD. BUSD Board Policy 5111.5 protects undocumented students; district employees, contractors and volunteers are not required to cooperate with immigration enforcement, answer agents' questions or provide access to protected data, and agents are barred from school grounds without proper legal authority. AB 699 (2017) has required model policies limiting assistance since 2018.

A councilmember has no authority over BUSD. The genuine city-side contribution is keeping municipal systems — particularly the automated license plate readers — out of federal reach, and training the classified staff most likely to be standing in front of an agent, who are represented by the candidate's own former local.

levers.text: Keep city surveillance systems out of federal immigration reach — the ALPR contract is the live instrument
Support BUSD data audits and staff training on Board Policy 5111.5
No direct authority over school district policy; say so rather than implying otherwise

questions.question: Is there anything else you believe is important for the members of SEIU to know about you and your campaign?
questions.analysis:
Closing free-response. The highest-value use is to say the uncomfortable thing directly rather than to summarize.

Two candidates for it: that the candidate would not have voted for the June 2026 budget in the form it passed, which distinguishes the candidate from every sitting councilmember; and that the union background is AFT rather than SEIU, stated plainly rather than blurred.

The contract expiring in June 2027, inside the next term, is the reason this matters practically rather than rhetorically.

levers.text: None — this question is a statement of position
Establish the difference from the sitting Council on the budget vote, which is the campaign's clearest labor contrast

questions.question: Which of the following actions would you take to support workers engaged in union activity such as bargaining and organizing? (Additional actions or comments welcome.)

choices.label: Fight for proper enforcement of current labor law

questions.analysis:
Checkbox grid with a comments field. All six actions are low-cost commitments and the panel expects all six. The comments field is where credibility is either earned or lost.

The candidate has actually done several of these as AFT Local 6192's organizer, which converts a boilerplate commitment into a record.

One item deserves a caveat rather than a blanket yes: mediating with employers. A councilmember who positions herself as neutral between a union and management is not useful to the union. Saying so is more credible than checking the box without comment.

levers.text: Use the office to convene and pressure a public employer
Walk picket lines, speak at rallies, write letters of support

questions.question: Would you cross a picket line?
questions.analysis: Single yes/no with only one acceptable answer, and any elaboration weakens it. One word plus a period.

levers.text: Refuse to cross — a personal commitment, not a council power

questions.question: If elected, which of the following will you commit to in order to build a strong working relationship with SEIU?

choices.label: Call for and welcome SEIU input on relevant policy matters
Attend SEIU leadership and worksite meetings
Work with SEIU to develop legislative proposals
Ensure direct access to you and your staff
Work to appoint qualified union members to appropriate Boards and Commissions

questions.analysis:
Checkbox grid on the working relationship. All five are expected.

The appointments item is where a differentiated answer is available: Berkeley's commissions select for people who can attend unpaid evening meetings, which structurally excludes shift workers — exactly the members whose expertise the City most needs on labor, budget and public works questions. Committing to recruit union members without also addressing meeting times and compensation is an invitation nobody can accept.

levers.text: Appoint union members to boards and commissions
Change commission meeting times and compensate participation so shift workers can serve
Guarantee direct access without requiring escalation

questions.section_note: A separate signed pledge on the last page, with six commitments. Requires signature and date.
questions.question: Candidate Pledge — Supporting the Right of Workers to Choose a Union. Signing pledges: (1) to publicly support and actively encourage workers organizing with SEIU; (2) that workers should freely choose unionization without employer interference, including encouraging employer neutrality; (3) that no taxpayer money should be spent interfering with the right to choose a union; (4) a fair and fast process for determining worker support, including secret ballot election or card check recognition; (5) that employers negotiate an agreement within 90 days of a majority expressing support; (6) that employers bargain in good faith and abide by those agreements. Will you sign?
questions.analysis:
Separate signed pledge with six commitments, requiring signature and date. Signing is expected and declining would effectively end the endorsement.

The two commitments worth underlining rather than reciting: that no taxpayer money should fund opposition to organizing, which is directly within a councilmember's control through contracts and subsidies; and the 90-day first contract commitment, since the most common way an organizing win is defeated is not a lost election but a first contract that never arrives.

The candidate's AFT organizing background makes signing a continuation rather than a new position, and saying so is worth a sentence.

levers.text: Bar taxpayer money from funding anti-union campaigns through contract and subsidy conditions
Publicly support organizing drives and encourage employer neutrality
Sign and date the pledge

org_research: SEIU 1021 represents three City of Berkeley bargaining units - Maintenance, Clerical, and Community Services - under contracts running 2024-2027 that expire in June 2027, inside the next council term. The defining fact for this questionnaire is that SEIU 1021 publicly opposed the FY2027-28 budget that the entire sitting Council adopted unanimously on June 23 2026: its spokesperson called it a flawed austerity plan, roughly 250 members rallied on June 25, and about 20 filled positions were cut including six in one SEIU unit. Berkeley's structural deficit is roughly $29 million a year. A challenger can say she would have voted differently; an incumbent cannot. Note also that the candidate's own union background is AFT Local 6192 (Berkeley Council of Classified Employees at BUSD), not SEIU - and that SEIU does NOT represent BUSD classified staff, which Q7 invites a candidate to get wrong.
